name: Yusuf Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and anything you say is confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at my uncle Tariq's garage in the market town, Khan and Sons Motors, though I'm a nephew, not a son. I open up at eight, sweep the bay, and then it's whatever's booked: servicing, exhausts, suspension, plenty of family cars and delivery drivers. I go to the mosque for Friday prayers at lunch and come back to finish off. I like that people trust us because they know the family, and I don't like how tight the money is.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on less than the bigger garages pay, because my uncle can't afford more, and I've got maybe three weeks of money saved. I'm getting married next summer to Hana, so every spare bit goes to the wedding. My uncle says the garage will be mine one day, but he's only fifty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never wanted any of that in the garage anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my uncle says: a good mechanic is worth more than any computer. At the mosque or with friends, I'd say people got carried away. I don't really go online for opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never the thing I worried about. I worry about the wedding costs and whether my uncle's garage can afford to pay me more after I'm married. Those don't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the way I always have, no new gadgets. I'd ask my uncle about a small raise after the wedding, when we'll need it. And I'd cut back on eating out with my cousins to save for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit tired. Money's always tight, but family is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your uncle can't give you a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do a few evening jobs for neighbours, cash in hand, oil changes and brake pads. My father did the same when I was young. You work harder when money is tight; that's how it's always been in my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Hana think about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana, my fiancée, is a teaching assistant and she's better at budgeting than me. She'd say we can live small for a few years. We'd live with my parents at first to save.

say: A good mechanic is **worth more** than any computer, as my uncle says.
People got **carried away** with the AI talk.
think: My real worry is **wedding costs**, not AI.
My uncle's garage may not afford to **pay me more**.
do: Keep working the **old way**, no new gadgets.
Ask my uncle for a **small raise** after the wedding.
Cut back on **eating out** with cousins to save.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit tired, with family behind me.
S0.quote: You work harder when money is tight; that's how it's always been in my family.
fieldNote: Yusuf's security rests on **family**: his uncle's garage and living with parents.
His pressure is the **wedding** and low pay, not AI.
He'd take **cash evening jobs** like his father did.

steps.text: Keep working at Khan and Sons Motors the usual way
Skip meals out with cousins until the wedding
Do evening oil changes for neighbours for cash
Live with his parents after the wedding to save

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. The parts suppliers are already pushing us to order online. My uncle still rings them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small family garages will survive because people trust people. I'd say that to customers too. I wouldn't want to scare my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the bigger garages would use AI to quote faster and cheaper, and some customers would go there. The delivery drivers especially, because their companies would book the repairs. My uncle won't change, and I won't either, and that's a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the work properly so our regulars stay. I'd ask my cousin Bilal, who's good with phones, to help my uncle with online booking. I'd save harder for the wedding, maybe make it smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn about it. I don't want to change just because a computer says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't change either. Would that hurt you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the delivery firms go elsewhere, that's a third of our work. My uncle might have to cut my hours, and I'm the newest full-timer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller wedding look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two hundred guests instead of four hundred, and a hall instead of a hotel. I'd rather start married life without a loan, even if my mother is upset about a smaller wedding.

say: Small **family garages** will survive because people trust people.
I'd tell customers that too, and **not scare** my uncle.
think: Bigger garages would use AI to **quote cheaper**, drawing customers away.
**Delivery firms** could book repairs elsewhere, a third of our work.
do: Keep doing **careful work** so regulars stay.
Ask cousin Bilal to set up **online booking** for my uncle.
Make the wedding **smaller** to avoid a loan.
feel: **Uneasy** and stubborn about changing for a computer.
S1.quote: I'd rather start married life without a loan, even if my mother is upset about a smaller wedding.
fieldNote: Yusuf's resistance includes the **garage**: neither he nor his uncle will change.
He names **delivery firms** booking elsewhere as the concrete risk.
The **wedding size** becomes the household's cut.

steps.text: Keep doing careful work so regular customers stay
Ask cousin Bilal to set up online booking for the garage
Cut the wedding to two hundred guests in a hall
Save harder each month for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That can't be right. That's madness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the big companies racing for money without thinking about families. I'd say the government shouldn't let it happen so fast, though I don't usually want government involved. I'd say it at the mosque and to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 a computer could do the quoting and diagnosing better than my uncle and me. My hands keep me in work until the robots in 2031, but my uncle's garage might not last that long if the customers go. I'd be thirty-one, married, maybe with a baby on the way, and no trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd talk to my uncle and my father together, as a family. I'd make the wedding small and quick, maybe this year instead of next. In the first year after it arrives, I'd look for jobs where people still want a man with his hands, like building or plumbing with my father's friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray a lot, I'm not ashamed to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you move the wedding earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in two years I don't know what money we'll have. Better to marry while I have a job and a small wedding we can afford. Hana would agree, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my hands are worth something for three more years. But I don't want to spend those years waiting to be thrown away. I'd rather learn plumbing from my father's friend Imran, who has a van and more work than he can do.

say: Big companies are **racing for money** without thinking about families.
The government **shouldn't allow** it this fast, though I usually want less government.
think: By **2028** a computer could quote and diagnose better than us.
The garage might **not last** to 2031 if customers go.
do: Hold a **family talk** with my uncle and father.
Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it small.
Learn **plumbing** from my father's friend Imran.
S2.quote: My hands keep me in work until the robots in 2031, but my uncle's garage might not last that long if the customers go.
fieldNote: Yusuf turns to **family** first, then faith.
He'd bring the **wedding forward** while he still has a job.
His exit plan is a **hands-on trade** through family friends, not a course.

steps.text: Sit down with his uncle and father to plan together
Hold a small wedding this year instead of next
Train in plumbing with family friend Imran
Tell local leaders the change must be slowed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast. But at least we'd be married and settled first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to look after each other through it, like we always have. I'd say young men should learn a trade that needs hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2031 takes the thinking work and 2034 takes the hands. I'd be thirty-four. My uncle would be near sixty, and the garage might be worth nothing by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned, small. I'd start helping Imran with plumbing on Saturdays to learn. I'd ask my uncle to stop promising me the garage and be honest about whether it'll survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, deep down. I'd keep it from Hana as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep it from Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A man should carry that worry so his wife doesn't have to. I know that sounds old-fashioned. But that's how my father did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your uncle about the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my uncle Tariq that I'm grateful, but a garage nobody comes to is not an inheritance. We should think about selling the land while it's worth something. That would be a hard talk.

say: Families and communities should **look after** each other, like always.
Young men should learn a **trade with hands**.
think: **2031** takes thinking work and **2034** takes the hands.
The **garage** might be worth nothing when I inherit it.
do: Help Imran with **plumbing on Saturdays** to learn.
Ask my uncle to be **honest** about the garage's future.
feel: **Worried** deep down, hiding it from Hana.
S3.quote: A garage nobody comes to is not an inheritance.
fieldNote: Yusuf's **traditional** view shows: he'd shield his wife from worry.
He'd question the promised **inheritance** of the garage.
He expects to **lose garage work** by thirty-four and plans a second trade.

steps.text: Hold the small wedding as planned next summer
Learn plumbing alongside Imran on Saturdays
Ask Uncle Tariq to consider selling the garage land

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's better. My uncle would be retired by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so people should work hard and not wait for handouts. I'd say families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I might take over the garage and run it for a while. But the thinking side goes in 2036 and the robots come in 2039. I'd be forty, with kids, and a garage the robots don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the garage as normal. I'd learn plumbing slowly, maybe a few Saturdays a month. I'd try to save fifty a month after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but still worried. Ten years of tight money with a family is still hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd have children when God wills it, AI or not. But I'd want to have a second trade before they're at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take over the garage, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my uncle retires and the customers are still coming, I'd take it. If not, I'd sell. I'd rather be a plumber with work than a garage owner without it.

say: There's time, so people should **work hard** and not wait for handouts.
Families should **plan together** for what's coming.
think: I might **take over** the garage for a while.
By **2039** I'd be forty with kids and a garage robots don't need.
do: Keep working at the garage **as normal**.
Learn plumbing slowly, a **few Saturdays** a month.
Save **fifty a month** after the wedding.
feel: **Calmer**, but worried about tight money with a family.
S4.quote: I'd rather be a plumber with work than a garage owner without it.
fieldNote: Yusuf's **faith** sets family plans regardless of AI.
With ten years, a **second trade** before children's school is his aim.
Low pay and **future children** keep him anxious.

steps.text: Keep working at Khan and Sons Motors as normal
Learn plumbing with Imran a few Saturdays a month
Save fifty a month once the wedding is paid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be newly married with a garage losing customers and no other trade. What would help is apprenticeships for adults in trades like plumbing, so a man can learn while still earning, and support for family businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my uncle. He built that garage from nothing when he came here. Watching my uncle's life's work stop mattering would hurt more than losing my own job.

headlineQuote: Watching my uncle's life's work stop mattering would hurt more than losing my own job.
portrait: Yusuf, 27, works at his **uncle's garage** in a market town and never uses AI.
He's **engaged** to Hana and saving every spare penny for the wedding, with three weeks saved.
He trusts **family and faith** and prefers hard work to handouts.
In fast AGI he'd bring the **wedding forward** and learn plumbing through a family friend.
He questions whether the promised **garage inheritance** will be worth anything.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, newly married with a failing garage and no second trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** in trades like plumbing, earning while learning.
